review_verdict: Owner-provided independent NotebookLM review: 20/20 Grammar +10/10 Writing Toolkit PASS; 0 mandatory corrections; no topic-linked lessons authorized.

entries.title: Present simple vs present continuous
entries.concept: habit/general pattern vs action in progress or temporary situation.
entries.use_decision: Choose the present simple for a recurring routine; the present continuous often emphasizes what is happening around now or is temporary.
entries.patterns: subject + base verb (-s/-es for he/she/it) vs am/is/are + -ing.
entries.example: Maya takes the bus every weekday. Today she is walking to school.
entries.contrast: The first clause is a regular habit; the second describes today's exception.
entries.watch_out: Avoid treating every now sentence as continuous: many state verbs normally take simple forms (I know the answer). Some state verbs vary by meaning (I'm thinking about the problem).

entries.title: Past simple vs present perfect
entries.concept: finished-time narrative vs past event connected to the present or an unspecified life experience.
entries.use_decision: Explicit finished past times normally go with past simple; present perfect can connect a past event to present relevance without locating it at a finished time.
entries.patterns: subject + V2 vs have/has + past participle.
entries.example: I visited Da Nang last July. I have visited Da Nang several times.
entries.contrast: The first visit is dated; the second statement counts experience without saying when.
entries.watch_out: Avoid I have visited Da Nang last July in standard teaching use. Present perfect use varies with dialect and context; do not claim all varieties express the contrast identically.

entries.title: Past continuous alongside past simple
entries.concept: background ongoing activity and a shorter event in a narrative.
entries.use_decision: Past continuous can set the scene; past simple can report the event that happens during it.
entries.patterns: was/were + -ing alongside a simple-past clause.
entries.example: I was drawing a map when the lights went out.
entries.contrast: Drawing was underway; the power cut is presented as an event.
entries.watch_out: Not every clause with when requires a continuous tense. Two past continuous clauses may describe simultaneous ongoing activities.

entries.title: Present perfect simple vs continuous
entries.concept: completed results/number of outcomes vs duration or continuing activity.
entries.use_decision: Use perfect simple to foreground a result or amount; perfect continuous often emphasizes activity or duration.
entries.patterns: have/has + participle vs have/has been + -ing.
entries.example: I have read three chapters. I have been reading for an hour.
entries.contrast: Three chapters focuses on output; an hour focuses on time spent.
entries.watch_out: Both forms can overlap; continuous is not always appropriate with state verbs (I have known her for years). Do not equate continuous mechanically with “unfinished”.

entries.title: Will vs be going to for future reference
entries.concept: predictions and intentions, interpreted through context.
entries.use_decision: will commonly expresses an on-the-spot decision or prediction; be going to can signal a prior intention or a prediction based on present evidence.
entries.patterns: will + base vs am/is/are going to + base.
entries.example: I think our team will win. Look at those dark clouds—it is going to rain.
entries.contrast: The second speaker points to present evidence.
entries.watch_out: Both patterns can make predictions; these are tendencies, not an absolute ban on alternative choices.

entries.title: Present continuous arrangements vs going-to intentions
entries.concept: scheduled personal arrangement vs intended action.
entries.use_decision: Present continuous often signals an arranged future event, especially with a time/place; going to can focus on intention.
entries.patterns: am/is/are + -ing + future time vs be going to + base.
entries.example: I'm meeting the club leader at three on Friday. I'm going to ask her about the project.
entries.contrast: The meeting is an arrangement; the question is the speaker's intention.
entries.watch_out: These expressions overlap; not every present continuous clause is future, and the arrangement meaning needs context.

entries.title: A/an vs the: first and shared reference
entries.concept: introducing one non-specific countable item vs identifying a particular one.
entries.use_decision: a/an often introduces one non-specific singular countable noun; the refers to an identifiable referent in context.
entries.patterns: a/an + singular countable noun; the + noun phrase where identifiable.
entries.example: I bought a notebook. The notebook has a blue cover.
entries.contrast: The second mention points back to the already introduced notebook.
entries.watch_out: a/an depends on pronunciation (an hour, a university). the has more uses than second mention; do not teach a fixed “first mention = a” rule for every context.

entries.title: No article vs the for general and specific groups
entries.concept: plural/uncountable nouns used generally vs identified referents.
entries.use_decision: A plural or uncountable noun can appear without an article when speaking generally; the can refer to a specific identifiable set or substance.
entries.patterns: plural noun / uncountable noun vs the + noun.
entries.example: Books can be expensive. The books on this desk are free.
entries.contrast: First is general; second restricts the group.
entries.watch_out: Some institutions, geographical names and generic uses of the follow additional patterns. Do not use this basic contrast as a universal article rule.

entries.title: Some vs any: neutral questions and offers
entries.concept: unspecified quantities in statements, questions and requests.
entries.use_decision: some is common in affirmative statements and offers; any is common in neutral questions and negatives, but neither distribution is absolute.
entries.patterns: some/any + plural countable or uncountable noun in these common contexts.
entries.example: We have some fruit. Do we have any bread? Would you like some tea?
entries.contrast: The last question is an offer, so some is natural.
entries.watch_out: any can occur in affirmative free-choice meanings (Choose any seat); do not label it always negative.

entries.title: Each, every and all
entries.concept: separate individuals, a whole set, and totality.
entries.use_decision: each often highlights members separately; every treats all members of a set generally; all can refer to the whole plural set.
entries.patterns: each/every + singular countable noun vs all (the) + plural noun where appropriate.
entries.example: Each student received a card. Every student needed a card. All the students joined the game.
entries.contrast: The first distributes cards individually; the others describe the whole group from different perspectives.
entries.watch_out: Avoid every students in this use. These are meaning tendencies, not perfect one-to-one translations.

entries.title: Few/a few and little/a little
entries.concept: quantity with countable plurals vs uncountable nouns, and the speaker's evaluation of sufficiency.
entries.use_decision: a few/a little often convey some quantity, potentially enough; few/little without a often emphasize scarcity.
entries.patterns: few/a few + plural countable noun vs little/a little + uncountable noun.
entries.example: We have a few minutes, so we can check the map. We have little time, so we need to leave now.
entries.contrast: The first presents remaining time as usable; the second stresses shortage.
entries.watch_out: Context and tone matter; a few does not guarantee a quantity is objectively sufficient. Do not merge with the pilot's separate many vs much reference.

entries.title: Must, have to and should
entries.concept: strong obligation/necessity vs advice.
entries.use_decision: must and have to can express obligation or necessity; should normally gives advice or expectation rather than the same force of obligation.
entries.patterns: must/should + base; have/has to + base.
entries.example: Visitors must wear helmets on this ride. We have to register by Friday. You should drink water after a long walk.
entries.contrast: The first two impose or report requirements; the third recommends an action.
entries.watch_out: must = personal and have to = external is not a reliable absolute division; negative meanings need separate treatment (mustn't vs don't have to).

entries.title: Mustn't vs don't have to
entries.concept: prohibition vs absence of obligation.
entries.use_decision: mustn't normally prohibits; don't have to says an action is not required, without forbidding it.
entries.patterns: must not / mustn't + base vs do/does not have to + base.
entries.example: You mustn't enter the laboratory without permission. You don't have to stay after the meeting.
entries.contrast: Entering the laboratory is forbidden in that condition; staying after the meeting is optional.
entries.watch_out: Do not teach mustn't as the negative of “it is necessary”; dialect and politeness can change wording, but the basic meaning contrast is important.

entries.title: Can and could in requests and ability
entries.concept: present ability and request politeness; contextual meanings of could.
entries.use_decision: can can report ability or ask for help; could may sound more tentative/polite in requests and can refer to past general ability.
entries.patterns: can/could + base; questions Can/Could + subject + base...?
entries.example: Can you show me the timetable? Could you show me the timetable, please?
entries.contrast: Both are requests; the second is often more tentative, not automatically more grammatical.
entries.watch_out: could is not a universal replacement for specific successful past actions; was/were able to and context may matter. Not all could uses are past.

entries.title: Zero conditional vs first conditional
entries.concept: general consequences vs realistic future possibilities.
entries.use_decision: Zero conditional commonly states a general regularity; first conditional often discusses a plausible future condition and outcome.
entries.patterns: if + present, present vs if + present, will + base (typical patterns, not exclusive).
entries.example: If water freezes, it expands. If it rains tomorrow, we'll practise indoors.
entries.contrast: One refers to a general pattern; the other to a particular future possibility.
entries.watch_out: Other modal/imperative forms are possible; do not apply the simplistic ban “never use will after if” across every meaning or construction.

entries.title: Second conditional and imagined situations
entries.concept: hypothetical or unlikely situations rather than a stated actual plan.
entries.use_decision: Use the common second-conditional pattern to imagine a different present/future situation and its consequence.
entries.patterns: if + past form, would + base.
entries.example: If I had more free time, I would join the science club.
entries.contrast: The speaker imagines having more free time; this is not a report that they currently do.
entries.watch_out: Past-form syntax does not necessarily describe past time. If I were... is often preferred in formal hypothetical use, while was occurs in some contexts and dialects.

entries.title: Comparative adjectives: -er vs more
entries.concept: comparing two entities on one property.
entries.use_decision: Shorter adjectives often use -er; many longer adjectives use more, with lexical and spelling exceptions.
entries.patterns: adjective-er + than / more + adjective + than.
entries.example: This path is shorter than the other one. This plan is more reliable than the first plan.
entries.contrast: The two patterns express comparison but attach different morphology.
entries.watch_out: Avoid more shorter in a regular comparison. Some two-syllable adjectives permit variation; good → better is irregular.

entries.title: Gerund or to-infinitive after common verbs
entries.concept: complement patterns selected by the main verb.
entries.use_decision: Verbs such as enjoy commonly take an -ing complement; verbs such as hope commonly take a to-infinitive.
entries.patterns: enjoy + -ing vs hope + to + base.
entries.example: I enjoy drawing city maps. I hope to visit the museum next week.
entries.contrast: Both describe activities but the preceding verbs select different complements.
entries.watch_out: Avoid enjoy to draw in standard use. Other verbs allow both with a difference in meaning (remember, stop) or little difference (start); this two-verb illustration is not a complete verb list.

entries.title: Defining relative clauses: who, which, that
entries.concept: identifying which person or thing is meant.
entries.use_decision: A defining relative clause adds information needed to identify its noun; who is commonly used for people, which for things, and that in many defining clauses.
entries.patterns: noun + who/which/that + clause in suitable subject/object roles.
entries.example: The student who designed the poster won a prize. The poster that she designed is on the wall.
entries.contrast: Each clause narrows its preceding noun to a particular person or poster.
entries.watch_out: Do not insert defining-clause commas here. Some object relatives may omit the pronoun; subject relatives generally cannot. Non-defining relative clauses follow different rules.

entries.title: Direct and embedded question word order
entries.concept: forming a polite embedded question without repeating main-question inversion.
entries.use_decision: Direct information questions may invert auxiliary and subject; embedded questions typically retain statement order inside the subordinate clause.
entries.patterns: Where is + noun? vs Could you tell me where + noun + is?
entries.example: Where is the community library? Could you tell me where the community library is?
entries.contrast: The second is a request containing an embedded question, so where the library is has declarative order.
entries.watch_out: Avoid Could you tell me where is the library? in ordinary embedded-question grammar. Not all direct questions use the same inversion pattern; check subject questions separately.

entries.title: Decide required content before optional detail
entries.process_step: understand the task and select relevant ideas.
entries.purpose: Apply Topic / Task / Must Include / Boundary to distinguish non-negotiable requirements from interesting extras; complement (do not duplicate) pilot REF-TIP-04.
entries.steps: Underline intended reader, action, facts that must appear, tone/length limit; mark optional details separately.
entries.worked_micro_example: For a fictional message asking a club leader to change a meeting room, mandatory facts are which meeting, new room, day/time; a long history of the club is optional and likely unnecessary.
entries.self_check: Can the intended reader act on the message without requesting missing information?
entries.avoid: Do not treat every personal preference as a required detail. This is guidance, not automated evaluation of a learner's draft.

entries.title: Brainstorm and select, rather than list everything
entries.purpose: Generate several plausible ideas and choose those that address the actual prompt.
entries.steps: Produce 3–5 brief candidate ideas; test each against the topic, audience and goal; retain 2–3 that can be explained clearly.
entries.worked_micro_example: For a fictional letter suggesting improvements to a school courtyard, shade, seating, litter bins are relevant; the writer's favourite cartoon is not unless directly connected.
entries.self_check: Can I say in one sentence why each selected idea belongs in this response?
entries.avoid: More ideas do not automatically mean a better answer. Never auto-score idea quality by counting bullets.

entries.title: Give each paragraph one clear job
entries.purpose: Prevent a paragraph from jumping between unrelated purposes.
entries.steps: Label each planned paragraph's role before drafting: identify the situation, give a reason or example, ask for an action, or close appropriately.
entries.worked_micro_example: In a fictional request to organize a recycling drive: paragraph 1 explains the request; paragraph 2 presents benefits and a feasible step; paragraph 3 asks for approval.
entries.self_check: Does every sentence in the paragraph help its stated job?
entries.avoid: Paragraph number depends on text length and genre; a short message does not need a rigid three-paragraph template.

entries.title: Topic sentence vs supporting detail
entries.purpose: Make the central point discoverable and support it with relevant specifics.
entries.steps: State a focused point; choose one explanation and one concrete, related illustration; check the illustration truly supports the point.
entries.worked_micro_example: A quiet reading corner would help students concentrate. For example, soft seating away from the busy entrance could reduce distractions.
entries.self_check: Is the topic sentence narrower than “The school is good,” and does the next sentence actually explain it?
entries.avoid: Not every literary or narrative paragraph requires an explicit opening topic sentence.

entries.title: Example, reason and evidence are not identical
entries.purpose: Distinguish an illustrative case, a causal explanation and verified external evidence.
entries.steps: Name the point; label whether support is an example, a reason or sourced evidence; avoid inventing survey numbers or quotations.
entries.worked_micro_example: A library may be useful after school because some students need a quiet place to work is a reason; a student studying there after class is an illustration, not a measured school-wide outcome.
entries.self_check: Am I presenting an assumption as a proven fact?
entries.avoid: A plausible example alone does not establish that a claim is universally true; reference content must never fabricate an external citation.

entries.title: Claim → illustration → explanation
entries.purpose: Make the reasoning visible rather than stacking connectors.
entries.steps: Offer a claim; give one concrete illustration; explicitly state how it helps justify the claim.
entries.worked_micro_example: A small garden could improve our courtyard. Students could grow herbs there. Caring for the plants would give them a practical shared responsibility.
entries.self_check: After the example, have I explained its relevance rather than assuming the reader will infer it?
entries.avoid: This is a flexible scaffold, not a universal paragraph formula or automatic argument-quality score.

entries.title: Address a reasonable counterpoint
entries.purpose: Recognize a relevant limitation without simply repeating the opposing view.
entries.steps: State a genuine objection fairly; respond with a proportionate reason or condition.
entries.worked_micro_example: A school garden would need regular care. However, a rotating volunteer schedule could make the work manageable.
entries.self_check: Does my response address the objection, or merely restate my preference?
entries.avoid: This is a reasoning reference; using however does not by itself demonstrate a successful counterargument, and not every genre requires one.

entries.title: Match email register to audience and purpose
entries.purpose: Use language appropriate for a friend, classmate, teacher or community organizer without equating formality with quality.
entries.steps: Identify relationship and purpose; choose greeting, request wording and sign-off that suit the situation.
entries.worked_micro_example: To a club organizer, Could you tell me whether the room is available on Tuesday? may fit better than Hey, give us that room!
entries.self_check: Would the intended reader regard the request as clear and respectful?
entries.avoid: Formality varies by culture and relationship; a friendly tone is not inherently incorrect. Do not score register automatically from greeting words alone.

entries.title: Paraphrase without changing the claim
entries.purpose: Change wording or structure while preserving the original meaning, degree of certainty and important facts.
entries.steps: Identify the source claim; rewrite in fresh language; compare actors, quantity, time and certainty between original and revision.
entries.worked_micro_example: Many students prefer quiet spaces to study can be paraphrased as Quiet study areas are popular with many students, but not Every student needs a silent room.
entries.self_check: Did I accidentally change many to all, might to will, or the time reference?
entries.avoid: Paraphrasing someone else's published wording may still require citation; this tool does not grant permission to reuse source text without attribution.

entries.title: Revise for task response, clarity and correctness
entries.purpose: Check more than spelling: required information, logical order, sentence readability and language accuracy.
entries.steps: Check (1) required details; (2) paragraph focus; (3) misleading claims; (4) verb/article accuracy; (5) sentence punctuation. Revise one concrete issue at a time.
entries.worked_micro_example: In a fictional event invitation, replacing It starts later with It starts at 3 p.m. on Saturday repairs a missing actionable detail.
entries.self_check: Would a reader understand the purpose and the next action without guessing?
entries.avoid: This checklist is self-guidance, not a claim that writing was semantically graded or certified. Trusted review is still needed for quality judgments.
